assessment.nobel_worthiness: Political economics gave a unified, formal framework for how electoral rules, constitutions, and state capacity shape fiscal policy and economic outcomes. It is a field-defining, widely taught body of work with a large empirical follow-on literature and strong links to growth and development.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the core of the constitutional and electoral-rule research programme and its synthesis. Besley is central to the state-capacity and political-agency strands. Other contributors, such as Acemoglu and Alesina, are outside this ballot entry, so the three-person limit leaves some attribution tension.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from the 1990s and the 2000s and has been confirmed repeatedly by theory and by empirical tests across countries. It is fully mature.
uncertainties: The 2024 prize on institutions and prosperity partly overlaps thematically, so the committee may see less marginal novelty.
The three-person limit may leave out other pioneers of the area.
Possible institutional proximity between some candidates and the Stockholm environment is disclosed here and not adjudicated; I have not verified it independently.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The political-economy model of trade protection (protection for sale), together with their work on innovation, growth, and trade, changed how economists explain trade policy and the interaction of trade with endogenous growth. Its influence on both theory and policy analysis is substantial.
assessment.attribution: Grossman and Helpman are the natural pair. Their joint contributions are clearly identifiable and have a long record of co-authorship.
assessment.maturity: The work is decades old, thoroughly confirmed, and absorbed into textbooks and empirical work. It is fully mature.
uncertainties: Trade has received a prize before, and the committee may weigh Helpman's overlap with the firm-heterogeneity entry B020.
Part of the empirical validation of the protection-for-sale model has been mixed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Their model of credit cycles shows how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks. It underpins much modern macro-financial modelling, including the analysis of the financial crisis, and is a strong complement to the recognised work on banking and financial crises.
assessment.attribution: The 1997 Kiyotaki–Moore paper is a single, clearly attributable contribution by two people. The wider financial-accelerator literature (Bernanke, Gertler, Gilchrist) is partly recognised already by the 2022 prize, and Gertler and Gilchrist are listed on the ballot but not proposed here.
assessment.maturity: The work is nearly three decades old, widely used, and confirmed by a large body of quantitative macro-finance research. It is mature.
uncertainties: The 2022 prize on banks and financial crises may be seen as having covered part of the theme.
The case rests largely on one landmark paper, with later work building on it by others.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework, with nominal rigidities, forward-looking monetary-policy analysis, and the Taylor rule, is the workhorse of central-bank analysis. Its effect on practice and on theory is very large.
assessment.attribution: Attribution is the main difficulty. Calvo, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets, Gertler, and others also made central contributions, and the three-person limit forces hard choices. Woodford (the synthesis and optimal policy), Gali (the canonical model and empirical work), and Taylor (policy rules) are a defensible but contestable trio.
assessment.maturity: The framework has been developed over thirty years and is used in practice. It is fully mature.
uncertainties: Credit among Calvo, Taylor, Woodford, Gali, Christiano, and Eichenbaum is contestable.
The framework's performance during the post-2020 inflation, and its treatment of heterogeneity, have drawn criticism.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The alternating-offers model of bargaining (Rubinstein 1982) is a cornerstone of non-cooperative game theory. It gives a tractable foundation for bargaining and decentralised markets, with wide applications in labour, search, and political economy.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein is clearly the central figure. Wolinsky's work on bargaining in markets is an important extension. Binmore's contribution is real but secondary to the proposal.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from the early 1980s and the late 1980s and has been confirmed over several decades. It is fully mature.
uncertainties: Recent game-theory prizes, in 2005, 2007, and 2020, may reduce the committee's appetite for another in this area.
The age of the main work may count for or against, depending on how the committee weighs timing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamic panel GMM estimators are among the most used tools in applied economics, with very large citation counts and methodological influence across growth, labour, and corporate-finance work.
assessment.attribution: The Arellano–Bond (1991) and Arellano–Bover/Blundell–Bond (1995, 1998) papers define the method. Blundell's wider contributions, such as structural labour supply and microeconometrics, are substantial, but here the credit centres on the estimators.
assessment.maturity: The methods are mature, widely used, and well understood. Known weaknesses, such as instrument proliferation, are documented.
uncertainties: The committee may prefer a contribution with a clearer substantive discovery than a widely used method.
Other contributors to GMM and panel methods, such as Hansen and Anderson–Hsiao, are outside this entry.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data have produced new, policy-relevant measurements of intergenerational mobility and of the importance of place and childhood environment. This links directly to the economics of inequality, mobility, and public policy.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the leading figure. Hendren and Friedman are core collaborators on the key papers. Katz's contribution, for example on the Moving to Opportunity analysis, is also significant, so the choice among the four is uncertain.
assessment.maturity: The key results are from roughly 2014 onward. Replication is encouraging, but long-run confirmation and the evaluation of policy implications are still developing.
uncertainties: The work is relatively recent compared with other candidates.
The causal interpretation of place effects, and the policy lessons, are still being debated.
Credit among Chetty, Hendren, Friedman, and Katz is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantile regression extended regression analysis to the whole conditional distribution, making it possible to study heterogeneous effects and inequality. It is a widely used and conceptually important econometric tool.
assessment.attribution: The Koenker–Bassett (1978) paper is the clear origin. Koenker built the field around it afterwards. Chernozhukov's contributions concern later inference and high-dimensional extensions and also appear in B007.
assessment.maturity: The method is more than four decades old, has been extensively confirmed, and is standard in both theory and applied work. It is mature.
uncertainties: The committee may weigh the method's wide use against its role in subfields beyond economics.
Econometrics prizes are relatively infrequent, and the 2021 prize partly covered the causal-inference area.
